passage:
Monday. Abhinav pinned his week above the desk: maths and chemistry blocks, one empty evening marked "spare", and lights out at 10:30 every night, written in the same ink as the chapters.
Thursday. The team bus broke down on the way back from the away match, and he got home at nine with the maths block untouched. He looked at the chart, crossed nothing out, and wrote beside it: "Away days need a lighter plan." The maths moved to the spare evening. He was asleep by 10:40.
The following Monday. His classmate Nandini yawned through the unit test after two late nights. "How are you so calm?" she asked. "I missed a day too," Abhinav said. "I just had somewhere to put it."

qa.q: What did Abhinav write beside the chart on Thursday?
qa.a: "Away days need a lighter plan."

qa.q: What does Abhinav's calm note on Thursday suggest about how he thinks of the missed block?
qa.a: He treats it as useful information about away days rather than a failure to feel bad about.

qa.q: Which choice in the Monday plan made Thursday easy to handle?
qa.a: Leaving one evening marked "spare" gave the missed maths somewhere to go, so no sleep was lost.

qa.q: How might Nandini see Abhinav's way of planning after the test?
qa.a: She may be curious or a little envious, since her late nights left her yawning while his slack kept him calm.

grounding: A teenager builds a spare evening and a fixed bedtime into his study plan, so a missed day becomes information rather than failure.

passage:
Nikita, put the highlighter down a minute and listen to your old aunty. When I was sixteen in Aizawl, I had my exam plan in a school notebook, every single day filled. The first time I missed a day, because rain washed out the road to the tuition centre, I cried as if I had failed the exam itself. My grandfather looked at the notebook, and he asked, "Why is there no empty page?" So I began leaving Saturday afternoons blank. When I missed a day, I asked what had got in the way instead of calling myself lazy. And I wrote "sleep" into the plan like a subject. I didn't top the class. But I didn't break, and I passed everything. So, what is your blank page?
Your Lalremsiami aunty

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami miss a day of her plan at sixteen?
qa.a: Rain washed out the road to the tuition centre.

qa.q: What did young Lalremsiami feel the first time she missed a day, and why?
qa.a: She was so upset that she cried as if she had failed the exam itself, because her plan left no room for anything to go wrong.

qa.q: What changed after her grandfather's question?
qa.a: She left Saturday afternoons blank, asked what got in the way instead of calling herself lazy, and wrote sleep in like a subject.

qa.q: How might Nikita take the aunt's closing question?
qa.a: Nikita may feel gently nudged to find room for rest in their own plan, rather than feeling told off.

grounding: An aunt recalls learning as a teenager to leave slack in her plan, treat a missed day as information and count sleep as part of the plan.

passage: The drilling next door started at eight on Wednesday and didn't stop. Vasudha tried earplugs, then the balcony, then the stairwell. By six she had done one of her three planned maths chapters. Last year she would have stayed up till two to finish. Instead she opened her planner, wrote 'noise day, 1 of 3' beside Wednesday, and moved the other two chapters into Sunday's empty buffer box, which was there for exactly this. Underneath she added: 'Drilling all week. Library tomorrow?' Preeti messaged at ten: 'Night study at mine? We'll finish everything tonight!' Vasudha smiled at the phone. 'Sleep is on my timetable too. Library at nine?' She switched off the lamp at half past ten.

qa.q: How many of her three maths chapters did Vasudha finish on Wednesday?
qa.a: One.

qa.q: What does Vasudha smiling at Preeti's message suggest she felt?
qa.a: She felt calm and steady, touched by the offer but secure enough in her plan to choose sleep.

qa.q: Which part of Vasudha's plan helped most on a bad day, and why?
qa.a: The empty buffer box on Sunday; it let her move the missed chapters without panic or an all-nighter.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel about Vasudha's reply?
qa.a: Preeti might be a little disappointed, but the library offer keeps them studying together without losing sleep.

grounding: Shows a teenager who builds slack into a study plan, treats a noisy, lost day as information rather than failure, and keeps sleep in the plan.

passage: Aditi's streak chart on the fridge in their Hyderabad flat had three empty boxes in a row: Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday. Her younger brother pointed. 'You broke it!' The old Aditi would have torn the chart down. Instead she sat at the dining table and studied the gaps. All three were rehearsal days for the school's Kuchipudi show, when she got home at eight with aching feet. 'So it's not that I'm lazy,' she told Salma on the phone. 'Forty-five minutes on rehearsal days was never real.' She redrew the chart: forty-five minutes on free days, fifteen on rehearsal days, and a line at the bottom in red: lights out 10.30. 'Fifteen minutes counts?' Salma asked. 'Fifteen every day beats forty-five sometimes,' Aditi said.

qa.q: Which days were the empty boxes on Aditi's chart?
qa.a: Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel looking at the gaps, compared with the old Aditi?
qa.a: She felt calm and curious rather than guilty, studying the gaps for a pattern instead of tearing the chart down.

qa.q: What did Aditi learn from the missed days, and how did she use it?
qa.a: They were all rehearsal days, so she set a realistic fifteen minutes for those days and kept a fixed lights-out time.

qa.q: Why might Salma ask whether fifteen minutes counts?
qa.a: Salma may think study only matters in long blocks, and be surprised that Aditi values doing a little every day.

grounding: Shows a teenager who treats missed study days as information, builds a realistic plan with a fixed bedtime, and values consistency over perfection.

passage:
'Lokesh, lights off at ten? Your test is tomorrow.'
'That's the plan, Papa. Sleep is in it.'
'In my day we studied till the milkman came.'
'And did it work?'
Ramesh laughed. 'Sometimes.'
'I wrote down every day I missed this month. Look. Monday I planned five hours after tuition. I did one. Wednesday, same.'
'So you were lazy on Mondays and Wednesdays?'
'No. Tuition finishes at seven on those days. Five hours was never possible. Now I plan one hour on those days and more on Saturday. Every day since, I've done what the plan says.'
Ramesh looked at his son's notebook, columns of small ticks. 'Every day?'
'Not perfectly. But every day.'
'Hm.' Ramesh switched off the light himself. 'Goodnight, planner sahib.'

qa.q: What time does tuition finish on Mondays and Wednesdays?
qa.a: At seven.

qa.q: What does Lokesh's calm reply to 'lazy' show about how he feels about the missed days?
qa.a: He feels settled, not guilty; he treats the missed days as information about his tuition schedule, not proof of laziness.

qa.q: Why is Lokesh's change to one hour on tuition days sensible?
qa.a: It fits the plan to real life so he can keep it every day; consistency counts for more than an impossible five hours.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel as he switches off the light himself?
qa.a: Ramesh seems amused and a little impressed, even proud, won over by his son's plan.

grounding: Shows a teenager who keeps a realistic plan with sleep built in, reads missed days as information, and values consistency over perfection.

passage: Last year, I finally learnt how to plan without breaking myself. I'm Ishita. In Class 10 my friend Jasleen and I both made huge timetables. Jasleen followed hers perfectly, pulling all-nighters, until she got sick a week before the boards. I built mine differently. Every Wednesday evening was blank, a buffer. Sunday afternoons were off. Lights out at ten-thirty, no matter what. When my cousin's wedding took two days in February, I didn't panic. I looked at what I'd missed, moved it into the buffers and carried on. A missed day just told me I'd planned too tight. I didn't top the class, but I studied steadily every week, and I walked into the exams rested.

qa.q: What did Ishita leave blank every Wednesday evening?
qa.a: A buffer, left blank.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel when the wedding took two days?
qa.a: Ishita felt calm, not panicked, seeing the missed days as something to adjust for.

qa.q: What makes Ishita's plan a wise balance of effort and rest?
qa.a: It builds in slack, protects sleep, treats a missed day as information and values consistency over perfection.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel comparing her boards preparation with Ishita's?
qa.a: Jasleen may feel exhausted and regretful, having burned out after all-nighters while Ishita stayed rested.

grounding: Shows a teenager who keeps a plan with slack, treats a missed day as information, values consistency over perfection and makes sleep part of the plan.
